text: Lesson 29 designed Meridian's architecture -- a segmented cardholder-data environment, tokenization, hardware-key MFA, and SIEM correlation. This lab turns that design into the two artifacts a real GRC program actually runs on: a quantified risk register, and a compliance mapping table, built together instead of treated as two separate projects handed to two separate teams.

Instead of scoring a risk as Likelihood 4, Impact 3 on a 5 by 5 matrix, this lab estimates it with FAIR, Chapter 3's quantitative method: a Loss Event Frequency range of 0.1 to 0.4 times a year, and a Probable Loss Magnitude range from $180,000 to $2,100,000 per event, covering regulatory fines, forensic investigation, and estimated customer churn.

Multiplying those ranges gives an Annualized Loss Expectancy from $18,000 to $840,000 -- a real range a CFO can compare against a control's actual cost, instead of a misleadingly precise single number. Hardware-key MFA at $40,000 a year is a clear, defensible spend against that range, in a way a bare heat-map color never could justify on its own.

The register entry writes down the risk, the FAIR range, the treatment decision, the control that addresses it, and the residual risk stated honestly -- MFA helps a great deal, but a help-desk account-reset process is still a real, unresolved gap. Writing that down plainly is what keeps a risk register trustworthy instead of quietly overstating how protected Meridian really is.

That same one control -- hardware-key MFA on privileged CDE access -- gets mapped to SOC 2 CC6.1, ISO 27001 A.8.5, and PCI DSS Requirement 8.4 at once. One evidence package serves three audits, instead of collecting the same proof three separate times under three different labels.

A real register repeats this structure across a dozen or more rows -- that repeatability, not any single entry, is what a mature GRC program actually delivers. Lesson 31 shows what still gets missed even when every one of those audits comes back clean.
